uncitedSentences.sentence: Research on automated written corrective feedback (AWCF) in second-language (L2) writing has expanded rapidly, yet the evidence base remains uneven across three outcome domains: accuracy, revision behaviour, and learner engagement.
This review synthesises the project library's coverage of AWCF relative to teacher-provided feedback, drawing on studies indexed in the supplied corpus.

content.text: A central concern is whether AWCF can detect the errors that matter pedagogically. Hyland (2025) argues that ChatGPT's lower frequency of stance features leaves it unable to offer accurate rhetorical and pragmatic feedback. Detection capacity is also shaped by how tools are prompted. Luo et al. (2025) found that ChatGPT's precision remained high across prompts (94%, 98%, and 94%) while recall rose considerably with prompt sophistication (10%, 33%, and 55%), and that ChatGPT overtook Grammarly on four high-frequency error categories yet lagged on five others.

content.text: Revision behaviour and engagement present a different picture. Zhang and Hyland (2018) documented one student resubmitting 13 times with scores rising from 79 to 90, against another who resubmitted once in under 14 minutes; they also found teacher feedback addressed more error types (16) than AWCF (8), though assignment differences may have confounded this. Zhang and Hyland (2021) reported that 88% of 33 students submitted more than five times (M = 9.5, SD = 4.07), yet some students disengaged, treating the revision cycle as overkill. Teachers' own positioning towards AWCF is similarly unsettled. Koltovskaia (2022) found no division of labour among teachers using Grammarly, with four of six positive and two sceptical, but the study captured only one-time use in a hypothetical scenario.
